title: Revisor 11+ English — Paper 1
notes: Passage and all items original. Two marking layers: 'auto' items are exact-match or numeric and mark themselves; 'rubric' items carry band descriptors for tutor or LLM marking. Passage text written to the specification implied by the questions (retrieval answers, vocabulary contexts and the phrases quoted in the model answers); replace with the author's original if supplied.

questions.prompt: Why does Ivy say that the counting 'had stopped meaning anything'? Answer in a full sentence.

bands.descriptor: Identifies that Ivy has done it so many times it has become automatic or habitual, AND links this to how familiar or routine the lamplighter's round is to her.
Identifies repetition or habit, but does not connect it to her long familiarity with the routine.
Retells the passage without explaining, or misreads the phrase.

questions.model_answer: Ivy has counted the lamps so often over the years that the number has become automatic to her, which shows how completely familiar the routine has become.

questions.prompt: 'He stood at the foot of it with his hand flat against the post, the way you might put a hand on a horse that had gone lame.' Explain how this comparison helps the reader understand how Mr Ashby feels about the broken lamp.

bands.descriptor: Identifies the simile and explains that comparing the lamp to a living animal shows Mr Ashby treats the lamps as something he cares for, not just equipment; notes the tenderness or sadness implied by the gesture, and may note that a lame horse cannot be easily mended.
Identifies the comparison to a horse and makes one clear point about care, affection or sadness, with reference to the text.
Notices the comparison but explains it only in general terms, or asserts a feeling without linking it to the image.
No relevant comment on the comparison.

questions.model_answer: Comparing the lamp to a lame horse makes it seem alive rather than mechanical, suggesting Mr Ashby feels affection for the lamps and treats them almost as animals in his care. Resting a hand on a lame horse is a gesture of sympathy for something that cannot easily be mended, which hints that he is sad and perhaps knows the damage is serious.

questions.prompt: What impression do you get of Mr Ashby from this passage? Support your answer with evidence from the text.

bands.descriptor: Three or more distinct impressions (e.g. methodical/precise; patient and unhurried; caring towards his work; reserved but not unfriendly), each supported by specific evidence, with some comment on how the evidence creates that impression.
Two or three impressions with mostly appropriate supporting evidence.
One or two impressions with some textual support, or several impressions asserted with thin evidence.
A single general impression with little or no evidence.
No relevant impression, or pure retelling.

credit_points: Methodical and exact — 'always four' rungs, never hurries, never stops
Long-serving and constant — nobody can remember a time before him
Cares about the work — the hand on the post, the long time spent on the broken lamp
Reserved but kind — returns Ivy's wave rather than ignoring her
Carries on regardless — completes the remaining lamps after the failure

questions.model_answer: Mr Ashby comes across as careful and methodical: he climbs 'four rungs — always four' and the narrator says he 'never hurried and he never stopped', which suggests a man who has done the same job the same way for years. He also seems to care about the lamps rather than simply working on them, since he spends a long time at the seventh and rests his hand on the post as though comforting an injured animal. Despite this he is not unfriendly — when Ivy waves he lifts his own hand back, which suggests a quiet, reserved kindness.

questions.prompt: In the final section of the passage, from 'Her grandmother came in with the tea things' to the end, how does the writer suggest that something is coming to an end? You should write about the grandmother's words and behaviour, and about Ivy's thoughts in the last paragraph.

bands.descriptor: Sustained analysis drawing on both the grandmother and Ivy. Recognises what the grandmother does not say directly ('Or somebody will'; 'they'll not stop there'), notes the gap between her casual tone and the kettle put down 'harder than she needed to', and reads the final paragraph as Ivy sensing a loss she cannot yet name. Comments on effect on the reader.
Clear analysis of several details across both parts, with some comment on effect, though one strand is less developed.
Identifies two or three relevant details and explains them, mostly at the level of meaning rather than effect.
Identifies one or two relevant details with brief explanation.
Locates the right part of the passage but offers little beyond retelling.
No relevant material.

credit_points: 'the electric' at the Rothwell end — the reason is stated indirectly, never explained to Ivy
'and they'll not stop there' — implies the change will reach Calder Street too
'Or somebody will' — the correction hints Mr Ashby may not be the one to fix it
The grandmother's flat delivery contrasted with the kettle put down 'harder than she needed to' — she minds more than she admits
'something in her face changed, though Ivy could not have said what' — the reader understands more than the narrator
The dark gap 'like a missing tooth' — a small absence in something otherwise whole
The tea going cold marks how long Ivy sits, and the closing line turns a small mechanical pause into something she may lose

questions.model_answer: The grandmother never explains directly what is happening, which makes the ending feel more unsettling. She mentions 'the electric' at the Rothwell end and adds 'they'll not stop there', leaving Ivy — and the reader — to work out that the lamps in Calder Street will go the same way. Her correction of 'he'll see to it' to 'Or somebody will' quietly suggests Mr Ashby himself may not be there much longer. Although she speaks 'as though it were a matter of no importance whatsoever', she puts the kettle down 'harder than she needed to', which shows she minds more than she will say. Ivy's last thoughts turn a tiny detail — the pause before each lamp lights — into something precious, and the admission that she 'might not have many more evenings left to find out' ends the passage on a note of quiet loss.

passage_text:
Every evening that autumn, Ivy waited at the corner of Calder Street for Mr Ashby to come round with his pole.

She had turned eleven in June. There were eleven lamps in Calder Street — one for every year of her life, which had struck her as remarkable when she was seven and had stopped meaning anything a long time ago. She counted them anyway, under her breath, as he lit them. It was not really counting by then. It was closer to breathing.

He always came at the same hour, or near enough, as the light thinned over the rooftops and the windows along the terrace turned yellow one after another. Mr Ashby carried the pole on his shoulder the way other men carried a spade. At each lamp he set the ladder against the crossbar, climbed four rungs — always four, never three and never five — reached up with the pole, and brought the mantle to life. Then down, ladder up, on to the next. He never hurried and he never stopped.

Ivy had asked him once why he did not simply reach up from the pavement, since he was tall enough. He said you could not see a mantle properly from down there, and a mantle you could not see was a mantle you could not mend.

The seventh lamp had been troubling him all week. It stood outside the old dairy, and it had a habit of catching, holding for a moment, and going out again, as though it were thinking the matter over. That evening it did not catch at all. Mr Ashby went up his four rungs, came down, and stood at the foot of it with his hand flat against the post, the way you might put a hand on a horse that had gone lame.

"She'll want a new mantle," he said, to himself more than to Ivy. "I'll bring one Thursday."

The other ten lit without complaint. Ivy walked the length of the street beside him and back again, and by the time they reached the corner the lamps were burning steadily behind them, and the seventh sat dark in the middle of the row like a missing tooth.

Her grandmother came in with the tea things while Ivy was still at the window.

"They've got the electric in at the Rothwell end," she said. "Went up last month. Poles and wires, the lot." She set the tray down. "They'll not stop there."

Ivy turned round. "What about Mr Ashby?"

"He'll see to it." Her grandmother straightened the cups, and then, after a moment, "Or somebody will." She said it as though it were a matter of no importance whatsoever, and she put the kettle down harder than she needed to.

Ivy looked back out at the street. From the window she could see six of the lamps, and the dark gap where the seventh should have been. She had never told anyone the thing she liked best, which was not the lighting itself but the half-second before it: the pause when the mantle hung between nothing and light, and you could not yet be certain which way it would go.

She thought she might count that pause, next time, and see how long it really was.

She might not have many more evenings left to find out.
